title: Towns for the Levites, and Every Promise Kept
summary: The heads of the Levites come to Shiloh and ask for the towns and pasturelands Moses had commanded. By lot, the tribes give the Levites forty-eight towns scattered across the land, divided among the priestly descendants of Aaron, the other Kohathites, the Gershonites, and the Merarites. The chapter then closes the whole account of the conquest and settlement: the LORD gave Israel the land, gave them rest on every side, and not one of his good promises failed.
story: The tribes have their land and the cities of refuge have been named. One group remains: Levi, the tribe with no territory. The Levites now ask for what Moses promised them in Numbers 35:1-8, and each tribe gives up some of its towns so that the servants of God's sanctuary can live throughout Israel. With that, the division of the land is finished, and the narrator steps back to give the verdict on everything from chapter 1 to here: God has kept his word. These closing verses (43-45) are the theological summit of the book. Chapters 22-24 will turn from the land to the people's future faithfulness in it.
historical:
The list of Levitical towns has a close parallel in 1 Chronicles 6:54-81, with some differences in names that reflect copying and updating over time. For example, Gath-rimmon appears twice here (verses 24 and 25), and the Chronicles list has a different name in the second place, suggesting a scribal slip in one of the texts. Scholars date the list's origin variously: some see it as an early record, others as reflecting the administration of the monarchy, and others as a later idealized plan. What is clear is that several of the towns were real priestly centers. Anathoth in Benjamin was the home of the priest Abiathar, whom Solomon banished there (1 Kings 2:26), and later of the prophet Jeremiah, who came from a priestly family (Jeremiah 1:1). Hebron, Shechem, Kedesh, Golan, Bezer, and Ramoth, the six cities of refuge, are all included, as chapter 20 anticipated.

The priests, the descendants of Aaron, received their towns in Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, the tribes nearest to what would become Jerusalem. Whether by design or by the lot, this placed the priestly families close to the future site of the temple.
cultural:
The Levites were Israel's religious servants. The priests among them, Aaron's descendants, offered sacrifices; the other Levites cared for the tabernacle and, later, the temple. Deuteronomy 33:10 also describes them as teachers who would teach Israel God's rules and law. Scattering them through forty-eight towns in every tribe meant that people across the land lived near those responsible for knowing and teaching the law, and it meant that Levi's scattering (Genesis 49:7) became a blessing to all Israel rather than only a judgment.

The pasturelands (migrash) were the open land around a town's walls, used for grazing flocks and herds. Numbers 35:4-5 describes them as extending a fixed distance from the town wall. The Levites did not own the fields and villages beyond (verse 12 notes that Hebron's fields belonged to Caleb); they lived in the towns, kept animals on the common land, and depended on the tithes and offerings of the people (Numbers 18:21-24).
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1-8 narrate the Levites' request and give an overview of the four groups and their numbers of towns: thirteen, ten, thirteen, and twelve. Verses 9-42 list the towns in the same order, each group introduced with its source tribes and closed with a total, and each city of refuge marked with a note. The refrain “together with their pasturelands” is repeated after nearly every group of towns. Then verses 43-45 break from the list into a solemn summary built on the word all: all the land, rest on every side, none could stand, not one promise failed, everything was fulfilled. The summary deliberately echoes the LORD's promises to Joshua in chapter 1, bringing the whole account of conquest and settlement (chapters 1-21) to a close.

outline.t: The Levites' request and the four groups of towns
Towns for the priests, the descendants of Aaron

doctrines.note: The chapter's final verses state its theology plainly: “Not one of all the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed; everything was fulfilled.” God's faithfulness to his word is the foundation of the entire book.

The Levites were placed throughout Israel, supported by the other tribes, to serve and teach. The arrangement shows a community that gives from its own inheritance so that God's worship and word are present everywhere.

The LORD gave Israel rest on every side. Yet the book also knows that enemies remained and that later generations would lose the land. This rest is real fulfillment and at the same time a sign of a fuller rest still ahead.

words.note: Migrash, pastureland or common land, the open ground around a town used for grazing. It appears fifty-three times in this chapter alone, a steady reminder that the Levites were given the means of ordinary life, not only a place to sleep.

Nuach, to rest. The LORD gave them rest on every side (verse 44). The word looks back to the promise of rest in Deuteronomy 12:10 and to Joshua 1:13-15, and forward to the time of David and Solomon, when similar language is used again (2 Samuel 7:1; 1 Kings 5:4).

Naphal, to fall, and by extension to fail. Not one word fell to the ground, as the Hebrew idiom puts it. The same expression returns in Joshua 23:14 and in Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:56), making it one of the Old Testament's great confessions of God's faithfulness.

christ: Verses 43-45 are the book's strongest statement that God keeps his promises, and the New Testament picks up that confidence. Paul writes that all the promises of God find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Hebrews 4:8-9 notes that the rest given under Joshua was not the final rest, since God later spoke of another day, and it points to a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God. The scattered Levites, living among all the tribes to serve God and teach his law, also form a pattern the New Testament extends: through Christ, the great high priest, all believers are called a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), spread among the nations to make God known.

hard.q: How can the book say that God gave Israel all the land and that none of their enemies could stand against them, when earlier chapters say much land remained?
hard.a: The tension is real and visible within Joshua itself: 13:1 says much land remained, and chapters 15-17 record cities the tribes could not take, yet 21:43-45 says the LORD gave all the land he had sworn. Several responses are offered. Many readers hold that the summary speaks of what God had done, since he had given the land and broken the power of its kings, while the earlier notes describe what Israel had not yet taken hold of; the gift was complete even where Israel's possession was not. Others note that ancient summaries commonly used sweeping language and would not have been read as denying the details the same book reports. Some scholars see different sources with different emphases placed side by side. All agree that the narrator wants the reader to hear God's faithfulness first. The following chapters and the book of Judges then make clear that Israel's continued enjoyment of the land depended on its own faithfulness.

questions: The other tribes gave some of their own towns to the Levites. What does it cost you to make room for the service of God and his word in your community?
“Not one of all the LORD’s good promises” failed. Which of God's promises do you most need to trust right now, and what past faithfulness can you remember?
God gave the land fully, yet Israel had not taken hold of all of it. Are there gifts from God in your life that are real but not yet fully received?
